newsitem.title: GERMANY: German unions urge Buba to cut rates to boost jobs.
newsitem.headline: German unions urge Buba to cut rates to boost jobs.

text.p: The Bundesbank should slash interest rates to stimulate economic growth if the German government is serious about fighting unemployment, the Federation of German Trade Unions (DGB) said on Thursday.

High wages are not the root cause of continued record joblessness, the union umbrella organisation said, commenting on data showing a rise of 5,000 in February unemployment to a postwar record 4.316 million.

"Only annual growth rates of about three percent can turn this trend around. That would require a stimulation of the economy by the federal and state governments and the Bundesbank, as leaders of a growth initiative in all European Union member states," it said.
The cause of Germany's record unemployment is that more goods and services are now produced by fewer people, it said.
"There has been a total skewing of the socio-economic framework in Germany," DGB said. "Those who still complain about wages that are supposedly too high just want to drive their profits higher."
Wages are at their lowest as a proportion of the national economy since World War Two, it said. At the same time, return on capital is higher than in the boom periods of the 1970s and early 1990s.
Record levels of exports and stock markets also show that corporate profits are not being translated into new jobs, it said.

Public-sector investments already planned for the future should be accelerated, and the Bundesbank should signal its intentions to lower interest rates in a way that would spark the slumping construction sector, it said.

"The Bundesbank must leap over the shadow of its traditional ideas and take an example from the courageous Japanese monetary policy. There the discount rate has been 0.5 percent for over a year, compared with 2.5 percent in Germany," it said.
